utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left off discussing your statement of 1996, Witness, and on page 2 you say that in fact, the barracks were not targeted frequently and the civilians weren't usually targeted near the barracks, and a high angle of focus indicates that the targets in fact were civilians. Now, how can you say on the basis of the angle of targeting that the targets were actually civilians? Where's the logics of that on the basis of the angle of firing? How were you able to determine that they were civilians that were targeted?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the street, when I mention the barracks, they are the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I didn't ask you the name of the barracks. I'm just saying that how do you know on the basis of the high angle of fire that you can -- or elevation, that you can determine that they were civilians, since you are an expert?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether that was correctly translated in the statement, I don't know, but it does mean that on the basis of the angle of fire, civilians were targeted. I probably thought they were coming down from those facilities where the Serbian army was stationed. That was the only path that the civilians passed by the barracks, and they were targeted. The barracks weren't targeted because the soldiers had left the barracks, so there was no reason to shell it. Just the civilians passing by, and that was the only means of communication between the upper part of the city and the lower part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you can't say on the angle of fire and direction of fire that the targets were actually civilians.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said now was probably --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean there was a translation error?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll check it out in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, tell me this, please: On page 2 of your 1996 statement, you go on to speak about the killing of a little girl Nena Brkic [as interpreted] was her -- Elma Jakupovic, and you say that she was the casualty of random fire and that that is what you think. And in the one but last paragraph you say that some of the neighbours accused their Serb neighbours from a certain house of killing that girl. Now, tell me, please, was that an indicator that the problem of sniping, sniper fire, which quite certainly was one of the most terrible events, was manipulated to turn fury against blameless neighbours of different faith? So it wasn't a crime that they had actually perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right, and that's what I wrote down, and I said yesterday that I really was objective, and I insisted at the time because the neighbour said the shooting came from here, and we had Boro Stankovic, the best ballistics expert, with us. He's died since. But anyway, he was a ballistics expert, and we carried out a ballistic investigation and really did establish that the shooting couldn't have come from that house because the angle fire wasn't right and the trajectory of the bullet couldn't have come from that house. So we did this in proper fashion and established that. And according to our analysis, I would say and we would say at the time, the team said at the time, that it was non-selective firing at a civilian settlement according and judging by this angle and that it just happened that this bullet happened to hit that girl.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 3, paragraph 1, of your 1996 statement, when you say -- talk about the death of Elvir Brkic, you say, "As far as I remember, the bullet came from Miroslav Kromolj street and an old Serb was killed on the same day, an elderly Serb lady was wounded by a sniper around the same location. Now, can you say that this is being precise if you say that a bullet came from a green house? Is that a precise assertion on the part of somebody conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this in 1996, and I didn't have my documents to talk to the investigators on that occasion, so I assume that's how that sentence came to be there. But there is a report -- that's how that greenish building came to be included there. But as I say, there's a report, and as far as I remember, there is a mistake here. It was elderly Serb lady. I'm not sure whether it says so in the B/C/S. I think it says man, but it was an elderly Serb lady.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 3, paragraph 2 once again of your 1996 statement, you say that you visited an elderly man who lived, and I'm quoting you here, "In a flat which was shot at a hundred times, a hundred impacts on the flat," that that was intense targeting. Now, if the flat was targeted 100 times, wasn't that an ordinary exchange of fire across the conflict line or front line, or was it sniping fire? Why would a sniper have to fire at one flat 100 times? It's an exchange of gunfire, that's what it was, across the front line. Isn't that right, Mr. Kucanin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that flat is opposite Miroslav Kromolj street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it up at the front line, the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no BH army line there, and that building was in a sort of no-man's land and the man didn't want to leave his flat, he had been living there all the time. And we really did find bullet holes, that many bullet holes in the walls, not the shells and remnants of shells. We found bullet holes and were quite surprised to find that many. And we wanted to move the man from there, but he didn't want to leave his flat. And when we took him to hospital because he was injured on the occasion, we had to wait for him get ready for half an hour, to collect his things and belongings and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that at the confrontation line, the separation line between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this house was all on its own between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was an exchange of gunfire, no sniping.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not from the building the man was in. I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in all these statements you seem to have the number 100. You always have the figure of 100 in your statements. You say that after the police stations were divided into Serb and Muslim ones there were about 100 policemen left. Then on another occasion, you say the recruits were about 100 inspectors. Then the 2000 statement says once again that there were 100 different cases describing an incident. And then you go on to say that, "In three and a half years I spent -- I conducted more than 100 investigations of different cases." So is that a way you like to express yourself or was this number and figure of 100 really the figure that was present on all these occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's always a parameter to go by. It's a good thumb rule, and you say sort of 100. Now, whether it was 120 or 95 or whatever, I always said approximately, roughly 100. So it might be a coincidence, I don't know, that it seems to be 100 every time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you refer to different subjects, different matters. There's a coincidence, you say. Now, in your 1995 statement, for instance, and that's on page 341, the last digits, you speak about an elderly man who was wounded on the balcony of his flat and you say on the wall across the balcony there were about 100 bullets. Was that the same man you mentioned a moment ago with the 100 bullets?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that flat was the one that was hit 100 times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it means the same man. You're talking about the same man and the same flat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 1995 statement you talk about the investigation with respect to the wounding of a little boy, and you had established that he was shot by the aggressor positions from Przulj's house, and I'm quoting you there, from your statement. And then again on page 338, paragraph 4, you say the shots were without doubt shot from that position. That means that you established the place the firing was done from when you say without a doubt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However in the next paragraph you say: "I don't know what the results from the ballistic investigation were because each person on the investigating team has his own responsibility and compiles his own report." Now, I'm asking you how can you say with certainty where the shots came from if you don't know the results from the ballistics report in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an investigation is conducted on the site, on the spot, I write down in my notebook what we state out loud and what the members of the team agree with. Now, there can be certain differences of opinion on the part of the ballistics investigator. I don't have their findings. They go to court or to the prosecutor's office or wherever they're sent to. But on that occasion we did manage to establish, and we had grounds to do so, that there were two holes, two bullet holes coming from the same direction. And the ballistics expert has a piece of equipment, machinery, and he places two points on the two bullet holes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I don't want you to explain what a ballistics expert does, what devices he uses, but here you say that without a doubt the shots came from those positions, and then straight after you say that you didn't have a ballistics report. So what do you need a ballistics report, an investigation for, if it is not to ascertain where the shots came from? So without knowledge of what the report contained, you say without doubt that the shots came from that building. So apart from all the -- apart from ballistics reports, all the other reports are inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on the spot we were able to establish what happened, but I do give myself a little leeway and say that I would like to wait for the ballistics report. So that's all I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understand your explanation. Now, speaking about the boy's injury in paragraph 5 on page 337, you say the second bullet shot from the same artillery piece flew across the front of a cafe. How can you claim that the second bullet was shot from the same weapon that was used to fire the first bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters ask you both to pause after a question or answer before you continue. Otherwise, it makes interpreting very difficult. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this doesn't seem to be clear whether the second shot came from the same weapon, as it says here according to a witness. So this refers to the bullet, a bullet fired from the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You -- that's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I don't think that's what I actually said. I didn't put it that way. It says: "According to the witness testimony, it would appear that it was from the same weapon." But I think there were two shots and that that's what that refers to, not to two shots fired from the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be unclear. But speaking of the shelling of Trscanska street on the 26th of October, you say at the end of the page ending in the digits 338, the penultimate paragraph, that, "The direction from which a shell came could be ascertained almost immediately on the basis of experience and traces left on the spot." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, how come in your statement in the last paragraph on page 338 with respect to the shelling of Trscanska street, it says that the shell was fired from the west -- from a west north-westerly direction and in the next case it could have just come from the north north-west. So the same shell from two different directions, west north-west, and the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on this. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not clear to me either, but never mind. Let's move on. Now, on page 339 and 340 - and I'm giving you the last digits there - you speak of the shelling of the Simon Bolivar primary school, and then you say on that page, 339, paragraph 7, that on that day Sarajevo was intensively shelled, so intensively that the members of the UNPROFOR themselves, as custom would have it in situations of that kind, didn't turn up on time to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was the Bosnian Serb army that did the shooting from a position where it was able to see the school as on the palm on one's hand. You could see the children and people going into the school. Now, tell us, please, which people were going into the school?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not children, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which people could be seen going into the school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that here. Perhaps that's my omission. But in that particular school, the people had set up an improvised water pump and had set up some barriers made of old cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't a school that was actually being used, and it wasn't a question of children at all. There were no children. It wasn't a school functioning as a school; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The school was completely destroyed and devastated, and in the hall of the school, the people set up a water reservoir there, and the people who were injured were civilians who were going into that hall to collect some water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 339 and the first paragraph on the next page, you say that ballistics experts found the tail of the shell, carried out tests, and took very precise measurements. In several other cases as it follows from your statement, there were no ballistic analyses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever circumstances allowed, they were done. When it was not possible, they didn't do these tests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly what was the ratio between the investigations that were done and not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In majority of cases, these tests were done. Maybe in 70 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kucanin. Does this mean that if each shell is examined then one couldn't talk about any continuous intensive fire because you couldn't have a team of experts coming out to examine each and every shell and every target that is hit by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an investigation is done on the spot, the basic data are taken down. If there are traces found of the shell, the remnants of the shell, the tail fin, the crater that a shell leaves is examined, et cetera. These shell parts are taken to a laboratory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but if that is being done, an inquest on site, then laboratory tests and all these other examinations, doesn't that all together indicate it couldn't have been intensive fire? If each and every case could be so carefully examined under those very difficult conditions with a shortage of manpower and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most cases were examined in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's what I wanted to hear. Talking about the shelling of the 9th of November in 1993, 342, paragraph 6, the shell that fell on the school in Alipasino Polje, you say it was fired from the south-western direction. In the same paragraph further on, you say that ballistic expert Adnan Tuzovic told you that everything points to the conclusion that the position must have been in the north-west. So where did the shell come from; from the south-west or the north-west? Because that shell couldn't have come from both those directions.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two different cases, two shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So these are two cases. Thank you, Witness. Now, could you explain for me -- I have several questions. On pages 344 and 345 of your 1995 statement, you describe the killing of a man called Mile Vasiljevic, who was obviously a Serb judging by his name. Though because of the shooting, you couldn't even take away the body, and still less engage in the necessary analyses, you still feel that you were able to establish with accuracy where the shot had come from, and you say it was an area controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. And it says on this page: "As we had no protection, we couldn't do proper ballistic tests, but it was clear from where the shot had come that killed Vasiljevic." Is that right? And then you say that it was a 7.9 millimetre calibre bullet. And then you saw on Serb television - I assume you mean about Pale - that Vojislav Seselj referred to a 7.9 millimetre calibre and that he personally had fired at Muslims in Sarajevo on that day. And on that basis, you came to the conclusion that he himself had killed Vasiljevic. "According to the indications of our police, one can say that it was obvious that Vasiljevic was killed by Seselj." Is that what you said? I am reading what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you joking or do you really think that on the basis of establishing the direction of fire without any ballistic analysis and then on the basis of a TV statement, you come to the conclusion that it was quite obvious that Vojislav Seselj had killed this Vasiljevic? So I have to ask you, are you joking, or could you have said something like that as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the indications. And in view of all the events that took place on that day when Vojislav Seselj was at Grbavica, he wore a sweater with a particular pattern, he was on television wearing that same sweater with a Browning, and I remember he boasted, saying, "Muslims know best how they fared today." The only victim in town that day was this foreman Mile Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is how you come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of this was proven. These are just certain indications. It is not any conclusion, any firm conclusion or any finding. It's nothing. As for Mile Vasiljevic, the late Mile Vasiljevic, he was going from one side to the other. The witness saw him walking, and when he was hit, his right side was towards Grbavica, and he was hit in the spot described in the report. He fell. He was alive for quite a long time. He called for help. No one could approach him until we arrived, and with the help of UNPROFOR, we pulled him out. I have footage of that incident when we pulled out the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. So you were not able to establish what you say in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we pulled out the body, we saw where the entry and exit wounds were. And on the basis of witness statements and his movements, we came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kucanin. Now, please tell me, further on on page 349, third paragraph, talking about sniping from Grbavica, from the Metalka building the four skyscrapers in Meljvina [phoen] street and the three skyscrapers of the shopping centre, and I'm quoting you: "For a long time we couldn't establish that the fire was coming from those skyscrapers. We thought people were being killed with snipers from the Jewish cemetery. Later on, with the help of ballistic analysis, we established that the fire was coming from those skyscrapers." So you needed time and ballistic analysis to establish that the fire was coming from those skyscrapers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then further on, you say you discovered that the fire was coming from the skyscrapers because the killing of one man was coincidentally filmed, and this clip was later analysed and this helped in locating the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it helped, among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was so difficult to establish the source of fire even when it was coming from a skyscraper, and there are not that many skyscrapers in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously you first had to look around and then you needed expert analysis to be able to establish the facts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you an example to explain this. There were two crossroads that were in jeopardy. Containers were put there. People were always crossing at the engineering institute. The fire was coming from Trebevic, the Jewish cemetery, and Gornji Kovacici, and no one even dreamt that, for instance, a father of my friend was killed like that. Everyone thought the fire came from up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in view of the difficulty in establishing the source of fire coming from the skyscrapers, whereas on the other hand in a number of cases you referred to in your statement you say that without any problems and frequently without ballistic analyses, you were able to establish with certainty where the fire was coming from. So as both is not possible, tell me, is it possible to establish the source of fire after a serious and detailed analysis or can it be done offhand, as was done on a number of occasions according to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about shelling, the direction or the trajectory of the bullet can be established on the basis of the traces in the concrete. That is as far as the direction is concerned. Other ballistic analyses determine the angle of impact and the other detailed elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know anything at all about various actions by forces of the army or the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina on their own targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speculations along that kind is something I heard mostly on Serb television. I did not carry out a single inquest in the course of my career that proved that to be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say that you heard such reports on Serbian television, let me give you a source that is a non-Serb source, which makes the same assertion. On the 22nd of August, 1992, the London Independent says, and I'll read out what it says and tell me whether that concurs with your own knowledge or are these also speculations? "The United Nations officials and senior western military officers [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] some of the worst recent killings in Sarajevo including the massacre of at least 16 persons in a bread queue were carried out by the city's mainly Muslim defenders, not Serb besiegers, as a propaganda ploy to win war sympathy and military intervention." [Interpretation] And then reference is made to various confidential reports circulating at the UN in New York as confidential reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with these allegations. The suggestion is that the massacre of 16 persons in a bread queue was carried out by the defenders. Do you know anything any such incident? Is there any truth in these sort of allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for a more precise indication of the spot where the massacre occurred and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the well-known incident when 16 persons were killed in the bread line, queueing up for bread. And this was attributed to the Serbs, but there is every indication to believe that this was done by the forces and the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You remember that. It was the reason for the introduction of sanctions, the immediate cause or, rather, the excuse for them.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't told me where this massacre occurred. Which was the spot and the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just rather than go into an argument, because time is short, do you know of any such incident in which the -- it's alleged that the defenders killed 16 people in a bread queue? Have you heard of any such incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know of any single case of our own army killing our own people. I can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now running out. You've got time for two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Time passes very quickly, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a team of the UN close to the Kosevo hospital was an eyewitness in Sarajevo of a Bosnian crew positioning a mortar within the hospital compound, hitting Serb positions, then packing up and fleeing, upon which TV teams come to see how the Serbs retaliated? And then they give the explanation that the hospital was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they said that somewhere in their report, why not believe them? I'm not acquainted with those facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as you were a policeman in Sarajevo, who was the first victim, the first killing that occurred in Sarajevo? Is it true that the day after the referendum there was an attack on a wedding ceremony of the Serbs in the centre of Sarajevo where Nikola Gardovic, the bride's father, was killed and another priest? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that Nikola Gardovic was killed at the door of the Orthodox church and that he was in fact the first victim of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was killed at Bas Carsija and not at the door of the Orthodox church. The column was moving, the procession was going from Bas Carsija towards the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that killing for the Serbs send a message: In spite of the constitution of Yugoslavia and Bosnia, we have declared that we want independence and we can kill you now? Is that -- was that the first victim? Was that how violence started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a pure comment, it's a matter of argument and it's not a proper question for the witness. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have a busy schedule today, I'll do my best to be brief. Mr. Kucanin, I will just refer to two points from your statement from the 4th of September. The first page, last paragraph, where you said that, "After the division of the police, I have to point out that all police units sought to remain objective and professional in their work regardless of the fact that there was war waging around them -- raging around them." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then towards the end of that first paragraph on page 3, you say that: "A part of the reserve police joined the army." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the last sentence, you say: "The reserve policemen were not even issued uniforms. They fought in civilian clothes and in sneakers."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one further point in connection with your statement, page 4. Yesterday, you said that it was possible to leave the town freely, whereas in the third paragraph here you explain that in great detail, and you said: "The only way to leave the town was the well-known tunnel. I passed through it for the first time in October 1993, and I think it was opened a short time before that. The regular and military police controlled the tunnel on the city side. I believe that at the other side there was control too. We had cards like passes that were issued by the minister of the interior. I had a pass because I had to work on the other side. Civilians were allowed to leave, but in view of the tunnel, the number of people who left was really limited." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that you could leave the town freely yesterday. That was Slobodan Milosevic's statement. But I was saying that it was not possible to leave the town freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not without a pass, and only a limited number of people could be given such passes, as you stated here.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applies to the tunnel. Yesterday we were talking about other things. As regards the tunnel, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to leave the town without a pass?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean in general.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only exit was through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on your statements, but you said on several occasions -- in the long statement you gave between the 10th and 12th of November, 1995, you say that where the people fell casualty to snipers there was never any military operation taking place, and you repeat that many times. You say that where people were targeted by snipers and hit, there were no military operations going on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know or have you heard of the following people: Muratovic and Karavelic, who throughout the time were very well-known figures in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muratovic? Could you give me his first name, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have the surnames. Muratovic and Karavelic. How about Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Karavelic rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because a very respected UN observer who was here in court here a few days ago said that Muratovic had told him that sniper activities were organised fully and that, "when they kill one, we kill one," and that that's how the balance was maintained. Do you know anything about that? And also that the snipers of the Bosnian army or police shot at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. You're asked about a man called Muratovic and his statement. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Kucanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. Muratovic is a frequent surname in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I really don't know who the man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a policeman yourself, did you know that sniper activity on the part of the Bosnians was also organised on a reciprocal basis? Do you know that as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said in my statement that I worked in the -- in -- I was a plainclothes policeman, so my job was to prevent crime in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. By chance, there was another respected UN force member, Major Thomas, in court here recently, and I made a note of that, he said the snipers were under the control of the Ministry of the Interior. That means you. Is that true and correct, that the snipers were mostly under the control of the police force or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior, a member of which you were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be quite unimaginable that anybody could have said that, but I really don't know. I wasn't a high-ranking official of any kind. My job was to prevent crime and uncover the perpetrators of crimes. I would go out on the spot to make on-site investigations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you mentioned Markale, I don't know which, the first or the second, but you don't mention Markale in any of these statements, whereas yesterday you said that you knew for sure that at the Markale, the ones you mentioned yesterday, there was shooting from the Serb side. Can you explain to Their Honours how you came by that conclusion. That is my last question for you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having mentioned Markale at all yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you don't remember, then I thank you, and that's all from me. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, you were asked some questions about a shelling incident that you referred to in your statement made in 1995, in particular references in that statement to the direction of fire, and I think you said that you were unclear about the references. There may have been a problem. In that statement, you refer to a report that you compiled about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown a three-page document. Your Honours, I don't have copies of this. We've tried to obtain them in time for re-examination, but they haven't yet arrived. We will provide copies at a later point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document in front of you as being a photocopy of your report in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to the last paragraph of that report, and do you see there a reference to the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can read out something that I tried to explain a moment ago. The report or minutes from the on-site investigation and everything that was conducted, you have to keep documents of this kind and records of this kind. It is the only meritorious document. And it says here that it was established that from the north north-westerly direction a mortar of a 60 calibre was ascertained and that is what exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up in a tree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked questions about some observations recorded in your 1996 statement. When you signed that statement, did you in fact sign a version in the English language which was interpreted to you so that you could check its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read to you the relevant portion of that statement as it appears in that original English version. Please listen to it, and if there is anything incorrect in what you hear, please tell us. This is in relation to civilians being shot in the area of the Marsal Tito barracks. I read, for the record, from the -- I'll read the fifth paragraph from that statement: "The area on this street between the Holiday Inn and the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity was well known as a sniping area. It is difficult to give numbers, but almost every day there were casualties. On certain occasions, the targeting was so intense the whole population would have to use alternative routes. Although there is a military barracks on the other side of the street, the street itself is rather wide, and the sniper positions are well elevated, so the targeting was definitely at civilians. The barracks, in fact, were not hit frequently. Also, the civilians were not necessarily hit in front of the barracks. In particular, the high angle of fire indicates that the civilians were the targets." Is there anything in that paragraph which is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. High angle of fire means that they had to fire from those facilities, from that locality, downwards. Had the angle been lower, they would have fired at the barracks. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kucanin. Nothing further. Excuse me. Your Honours, in relation to the material tendered in respect of this witness, could I clarify that tabs 2 and 10 were tendered under seal. They should be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. And do you want the last report that you referred to? There was a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the incident of the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to admit that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't require that to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Kucanin, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While the witness is going out, let me deal with some administrative matters, if I may. If the legal officer would come up, please. There was a request yesterday that we renumber Exhibit D216, the witness statement of Major Thomas, but having thought about it, our practice has been to admit such statements as Defence exhibits, and that's what we'll do. We'll continue with that. So it remains D216. At some stage this morning we need to discuss next Tuesday's work. This may be a convenient moment to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to raise a couple of matters on the witness list but I think Mr. Ierace has one or two other matters to deal with before perhaps I can turn to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Would this be a convenient time to formally tender material which was admitted by the Trial Chamber by order of the 7th of October? It's material which relates to four witnesses from the Galic trial, some exhibits, and the transcript. If I give the four names and perhaps exhibit numbers could be allocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What I think we'll do is we'll do it one at a time, please. If you would give the name and we will give it a number. This is under Rule 92 bis, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are statements which we admitted. We'll do it one at a time and then we'll have them. Let us first of all get the numbers and then we'll have them. Yes. Would you give the first number -- the first name, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: First name is Carl Harding. There are seven tabs, all to be tendered publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps we can have those, please. Yes, the next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Eldar Hafizovic, six tabs, all to be tendered publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Milan Mandilovic, two tabs for public tender.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 599.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that 99 or 89?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 589. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the final name is John Hamill, seven tabs for public tender.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 590.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I address you on the witness listing in private session? And I hope that the other witness is being brought to outside court so as not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Colonel Franken, please. While he's coming in, his evidence is available to you in 92 -- Colonel Franken, please. His evidence is available to you in the form of prior testimony under 92 bis, which has been granted with cross-examination, and there's also a further short statement dated the 17th of October which deals with extracts from a video compilation and some documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust Your Honours have a binder. On this occasion it may be sensible if the binder is given four different exhibit numbers because, as you'll see, the different parts have different -- all start with tabs 1 and then sequentially. The -- if that's acceptable, then the first part would have the next exhibit number and is in, I think, ten tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next Exhibit number is 591.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following part, which starts with the full transcript of the video which we're not going to play, is in six tabs. And may that become 592?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Exhibit number is 592.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third part, which begins with the witness's 17th of October witness statement, is in four tabs, and may that become 593.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Three tabs or four tabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four tabs I'm told. I've only got three but I gather there's a fourth one. Yes, the fourth tab --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- is either with you or coming.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. The next Exhibit number is 593.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the last part of the bundle is in 38 tabs, and maybe that can become 594.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next Exhibit number is 594.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, with Mr. Waespi who is going to help me, we're going to take the evidence of this witness in chief extremely briefly and to have in mind, of course, that the accused has in his recent questioning acknowledged that terrible crimes were committed in Srebrenica, so that to some degree matters may not fall for debate that otherwise could have done. The -- just to give the most rudimentary context to the witness's evidence and make sense for those viewing, he was the deputy commander of the Dutch Battalion at Srebrenica between January and July of 1995, second in command to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans at the time. DutchBat, as it was known, being in the Srebrenica enclave for the purposes of deterring attacks, demilitarising the Muslims, and supporting non-governmental organisations and other organisations. Amongst other points that the witness has made in his prior testimony is that demilitarisation of those zones wasn't complete but then the witness says circumstances were so dangerous that he wouldn't have dreamt of handing over his personal weapons had he been in that position and obliged or invited so to do. In July of 1995, and I trust the Chamber has a summary from which I'm drawing some of this material, on the 11th of July, the witness received a report from B Company. It may be helpful if the Chamber turns in Exhibit 591, first of all, to tab 2, which gives a map of the overall area with which we're concerned. And perhaps the usher could lay some of these on the overhead projector to make sense of it as it comes along. But tab 2 shows the considerable area with which the Chamber is concerned when dealing with the crimes committed at Srebrenica. Srebrenica is, of course, here in the south of the map, south-east, with the border running up north-south and with points of materiality, places where people were executed and places where people were buried, right the way up some 40 kilometres past Zvornik to the north. Srebrenica itself is a town but the word is used to describe the wider area and you're particularly concerned, of course, with Potocari four kilometres or thereabouts, a bit more, I think, to the north of Srebrenica. B Company was located in the centre of Srebrenica town, and the other DutchBat base with which the Chamber's probably already familiar and is well known was at Potocari. And thus it was on the 11th of July that this witness was told by the commander of B Company in the centre of Srebrenica town that there was shelling on the town of civilians and indeed that B Company wasn't able to control its own compound, and the witness approved his request to abandon the compound there, which he did, moving to Potocari. At the same time, the road to Potocari being so exposed to attack from surrounding gun emplacements of the Bosnian Serbs that the witness organised a safe route for refugees to work their way through so far as they could to the Potocari base, and it was to protect the refugees so far as they were able that DutchBat was reduced. Should be borne in mind that there were as few as 150 combat-trained soldiers for DutchBat working on 16 per cent, or thereabouts, of the ammunition and arms that they should normally have had, they finding themselves now in the centre of a community at Potocari of some 30.000 civilians, some within their own compound, the others outside. The Dutch were threatened that if they didn't stop airstrikes which were being delivered elsewhere, that they would be fired on both in their compound and that the refugees would also be fired upon - the civilian refugees, let it be understood - and at this time, the Bosnian Serbs had already taken Dutch prisoners of war or Dutch soldiers as prisoners of war, and they were also threatened with death in certain circumstances. The VRS had some 35 pieces of artillery, including a couple of multiple-launch rocket systems at their disposal. On the 12th of July - paragraph 11 of the summary if the Chamber is following it - there was an attack on the compound at a time when the commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was meeting Mladic in Bratunac. Efforts were made to assist the refugees, and the witness organised escorts, but the sort of problems he faced at that time included the fact that the Serbs just took from the Dutch 15 or 16 jeeps. There's really no doubt, and the witness could confirm this, really as to who was in charge and how limited was the ability of DutchBat at that time to achieve very much of their mandate. The majority of refugees in Potocari were women and children, but there were certainly some 300 or so men in the compound and 5 to 600 men outside for whose fate the witness was extremely anxious because Mladic had told DutchBat that he was going to separate men from the age of 16 to 60 out from other refugees in order to check if they were war criminals. And so it was to happen that they were separated out, at least. And if we look on in the tabs of Exhibit 591 to tab 7, you'll see a photograph that is orientated south-north, not north-south. And what you can see here on the left-hand side, the white square, is a building just above or just actually south of the battalion's base at Potocari which would be just at the bottom of this picture. In the middle of the photograph you can see white rectangles, which are buses, and then just to the right of the big white blob but on the opposite side of the road there is a building which is known as the white house. And what happened was that men were being separated and processed in some way through the white house with a pattern developing of buses leaving with women and children and with men, the expectation being that they were going to go to places of safety or be transferred to Bosnian-held territory. The Dutch Battalion was only able to police the destination of these buses for a very limited amount of time, I think some four convoys and that was it, and the witness became extremely concerned about what was happening to the men who were being processed not only because it became clear at some stage that some nine men were seen to have been executed in a field not so very far away from the white house, but also because it became clear that although it was expected that the men would find their way to Kladanj, which you can see on tab 2 on the left-hand side, such reports as he was getting indicated that they weren't actually finding their way there. The witness took such steps as he could, including listing men who were within the compound and faxing the names of those men to Tuzla and to The Hague, some 251 of them, and I think nothing is known of what ultimately happened to them. The witness complained to a man called Colonel Jankovic about the treatment of the men at the white house, and Jankovic, while making no acknowledgements about mistreatment, nevertheless said that the VRS had 6.000 prisoners of war under their control, a number that, of course, relates significantly to the numbers of people said, as the Chamber will know, to have been killed in the course of the mass crimes at Srebrenica. Being no longer in control of the position, DutchBat did what it could but it didn't have anything like enough food and starvation was simply facing them if they were to stay where they were for very much longer. There was some water, but of course food for the 30.000 people around was something way beyond their control, and indeed individuals were committing and attempting to commit suicide while the situation developed. On the 13th of July, paragraph 17, the witness contacted a Colonel Acamovic. At that time they were the subject, impertinently, of a request for fuel from the VRS, which they declined. But nevertheless, in looking at the overall scale of the operation that can be revealed on that tab 2, if you look at the -- or pay attention at some stage to the code indicating burial sites and execution sites and so on, all a matter of course for the Chamber to decide upon, but the witness's estimate is that up to four or six brigades would have been required, I think, to mount the operation of separating, executing, and disposing of all the bodies. On the 17th of July, the witness met a Serbian delegation led by Colonel Jankovic, dealing with some hospital patients, and he was obliged at that stage to deal with a document which he required a field translation, which again suggested in some way that the evacuation now under way of the civilians had been handled properly. You can see that at tab 9 in Exhibit 591, and the field translation is the fourth sheet in where the witness, doing the best he could to limit a document that the Chamber may think is cynical, wrote at the end of it in hand the words, "As far as the convoys actually escorted by the UN forces are concerned," thus to qualify a document that the Chamber will see otherwise suggested that there had been a proper evacuation of civilians. I understand he will confirm that his making that note at the end of the document infuriated a Serb lawyer who was present on behalf of the VRS, but if I'm wrong about that, he can correct me. That's probably all I need to say by way of summary of his evidence before I invite Mr. Waespi to deal with the eight-minute video which he and the witness can comment on together. If I can take you at speed through the exhibits to make sure you're sufficiently familiar with them. At tab 3 of Exhibit 591 is the white house. Tab 4 is the list of men made by the witness, the best to secure their safety. Tab 5, is the man Jankovic. Tab 6 is the rather significant sighting of clothing and bags being burnt outside the white house which lies behind this picture. Tab 7 we've looked at. Tab 8 is a list of the wounded. Tab 9 I've dealt with. Tab 10 is Krstic. If we go to Exhibit 592, the first tab is the full video which is available and thus produced but we don't need to take time with here. Tab 3 is Lieutenant Colonel Karremans. Tab 4 Jankovic. Tab 5, Mladic; and tab 6, Mr. Boering, who may be referred to. Exhibit 593, Your Honours have tab 1, the witness statement, and then you have some of the reporting at tabs 2 and 3 from Mr. Akashi. Time deters me from -- or the limits of time deters me from taking you through that. Then finally in Exhibit 594, the last tab, 38, is the very limited range of comments by the witness in his adopting of various UNMO reports, and I think the only one I would invite you to look at which are otherwise an available record of events is tab 18 which goes back to events on the 11th of July and is a dramatic account from UNMOs of what was happening on that day, and I read half a dozen lines: "At this moment the stream of refugees and wounded is incountable any more. We figure that a total of 20.000 refugees came to the DutchBat Compound of Potocari already and is growing steadily. Since our last report, the shelling of the town has been going on despite the airstrikes. The town is in the hands of the BSA by now, and the latest ultimatum given by the BSA is that if the airstrikes continue, everything inside the enclave will be bombed, also UNPROFOR and the other UN organisations. B Company has left their compound in Srebrenica and is heading for Potocari." Thus the build-up to this enormous disaster and crime, and may I ask before the break, if I'm not being impertinent in suggesting that we may have reached that time, the witness one question in relation to tab 2 on the first exhibit. If he could look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's this, Colonel Franken -- actually, I think first of all I've forgotten to confirm that you are indeed Colonel Franken.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Franken, currently commander of the forces to the north of The Hague. This map which we've looked at which has its code indicating execution sites and matters of that sort, disturbed graves and undisturbed graves covering over 40 kilometres. It will be for the Judges in due course to decide, if they need to, whether these annotations are correct and whether executions and burials occurred, but if this is a correct reflection of the killing and disposal of the thousands of men from Srebrenica, what scale of operation was it? What number of troops would have been required?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: This operation is the coordination and participation of civil means as well. I mean transport means that, as far as I can judge, it means above corps level, so that means Pale level to coordinate, to plan this. So you need about two or three brigades, units to perform it, to execute it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That will be a convenient moment. Lieutenant Colonel, could I remind you, please, as we remind all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before turning to the video, for assistance in orientation, would the Chamber go, please, to 593, tab 4. It's now on the overhead projector, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, does this show again south-north, not north-south, the UN base, to the south of it, that's a little further up, the blue factory that we saw on an earlier picture opposite the white house, with lines of buses, seen as white oblongs on the road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those buses would have been going north, i.e., going towards the bottom of the picture on their various journeys?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I add one photograph that I intended to add, and maybe this could become tab 5 of Exhibit 593. The overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 593, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this show Colonel Karremans about to present himself to Mladic when the DutchBat finally withdrew?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, I think, were right -- you were the last vehicle out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was with the last part of the vehicles. I was commander of the APCs, the armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were able to be able to avoid having to speech to Mladic on the way out, by dint of that. We see some civilians standing there. I don't think you're in a position to recognise any of them yourself, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There is just one I can recognise, that's the second from the left in the light green shirt, this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is a person known to me as Petar. He officially was the interpreter of the UNMOs, but actually was used as interpreter by the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any case the men standing at the time looking at Colonel Karremans, you don't recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, I should have dealt with this: On the 17th of July at your meeting when the ICRC were having difficulties getting access for a vehicle of theirs across the border to Serbia, was Jankovic able to clear their passage easily by a single phone call?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the statement you made about matters which is the first exhibit of -- first tab of 593, you made this statement on the 17th of October. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi now, please, for video. Examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, there will be about 13 small segments out of video now exhibited 592, tab 1, and there is a transcript in English which is Exhibit 592, tab 2 in English and B/C/S, but, Your Honours, the video segments you will see are subtitled so you needn't bother with this transcription right now. The witness also explains what he sees on these videos in his additional statement of 17 October, and that's now exhibited as 593, tab 1. If the first clip could be played, please, and that's Srebrenica town, 11th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Colonel Franken, can you explain what we're seeing now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was quite a massive panic in the civil population so the refugees in the town, on the 11th they overran the guard of the base of B Company and you see here them here crawling across our trucks, et cetera, just to get out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move to the second clip, and if you could please comment on that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you can see on page 8 of the summary the reference to the 13 clips we are playing. The second one will be paragraph 6. I believe, Your Honours, we have a slight technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is in an additional statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you look at the statement, on page 2 of it, additional witness statement, it's dated 17th October, 2003. The paragraphs 6 -- 5, 6 until 16 discuss these issues. I'm sorry, Mr. President, but if you allow us, we have a serious technical problem. If we could move on to cross-examination, and with your leave we would like to play these clips later, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We don't want to waste any further time on it. We'll return to it, and of course the accused will have the opportunity to cross-examine on it in due course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I start the cross-examination, I should just like to make a remark to what Mr. Nice said, that allegedly I accepted some crimes in Srebrenica. How can I accept something I know nothing about? What I do know is that the police of Serbia, when it first learnt about somebody committing crimes, Erdemovic, in actual fact, who was tried here, was arrested as soon as they set foot on the territory of Serbia, and the accusation was that he had committed war crimes. That's what I know. Now, that I'm interested that the real truth be learnt, what actually happened, who stood behind everything, yes, I am, very much so, because it is in Serbian military tradition -- or, rather, to kill prisoners of war is the most dishonourable act that anybody could do. Now, the assumptions of what happened, if it happened as it has been purported to have happened, then I said that that could have only been done by somebody who was an enemy to the Serbs, to the Muslims, and mad to boot. So I wanted to make that clear. And, gentlemen, here you've been emphasising that the principle of the public nature of the trial is being respected, and this testimony is in open session, it is public, but I assume you're aware of the fact that this principle in presenting things in this way is cynical. What Mr. Nice has just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not here for speeches. We hear what you say about your position as far as your defence is concerned and of course we'll listen to that where it is of assistance. You will have, in due course, the opportunity to make your defence, but we will hear when you address us what is in dispute and what is not. Now, you begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. May, how much time are you going to give me for this witness, for my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You get an hour with this witness. He's a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I cannot cross-examine this witness within the space of one hour. Even if I skim over all the questions that I wish to pose very briefly. You know what happened. You know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us waste no further time on it. If at the end of one hour you need more time, you can ask for it. We will then consider it. And it will depend partly on the amount of time that is wasted. If you waste time, then you won't get additional time. If you don't, then we'll consider the position. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Franken, without a doubt it is morbid to calculate, using any kind of information, civilian casualties. However, I would like us to clarify things and have the truth about Srebrenica come out, beginning with the number of persons missing, number of persons killed, and to the fact to see whether my belief is that if the crime took place, what the extent of the crime was and that it could not have been planned. It could not have been the political and military strategy of Republika Srpska at all. And it had absolutely nothing to do with Serbia and Yugoslavia. So please, may I ask you to give me short answers to my questions and help me clarify certain matters. Tell me, please, Mr. Franken, do you remember that on the 21st of January, 1995, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed restrictions with respect to UN movement in the Bandera Triangle area and that the UN battalion decided to ignore those restrictions, and on the 27th of January, it took two patrols into that particular zone? However, the operation resulted in a response from the Bosnians, and they held 100 people of the battalion as hostages from the 27th to the 31st of January, in that period of time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct. Just have to remark that the situation of the restricted freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle already existed before the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. That just confirms what I've been saying. Tell me, please, do you know that the army of Republika Srpska exclusively responded to attacks from the BH army, and that at the end of 1994 and especially in 1995, Muslim military activities in the area escalated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can't say anything about 1994 because I came down there in 1995. In general, I had a situation given by DutchBat II, our predecessors over there. While both parties were not cooperating with the UN, which means not giving me the information who did what attack or whatever, I only could observe that Bosnian Serb artillery repeatedly shelled locations in the enclave. But there are two times that Bosniak, means Muslim, actions outside the enclave were reported to me. It was once in the northern area of OP Mike that's directly north of the enclave where one of my observation posts four in the morning burning houses. Two days later it was claimed by the BSA as a result of a Bosniak action. And once in the area down south, south of Zeleni Jadar, outside the enclave where the Bosnian Serb army claimed that seven of their soldiers were killed by a Bosniak ambush in BSA territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember that the attack on the village of Visnjica in which the houses were burnt and everything razed to the ground, the Serb houses that were there? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is the action I tried to describe to you being north of OP Mike. We asked the Bosnian Serb army to go over there and see what the consequences were, because the only thing we saw was burning houses. So what the damage, eventually killing or wounded on the ground were, I could not confirm or have any idea about that because BSA didn't allow us to go outside of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you know about the piece of information according to which some people were burnt alive in those houses, Ljubinko Vujadinovic, I have here, an old man who was burnt in his house, burnt to death. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I did not. And generally, I said before, I didn't know any details about that. The only observation I got was from my own troops reporting in the morning that there were burning houses. And trying to get more information from the BSA side failed because they only took contact two days later and said that we had to make sure the 28th Division didn't get out of the enclave and didn't give, even on our request, didn't give any further information, detailed information. So what exactly happened in that village is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now do you remember that on the 28th of May, 1995, when the forces also from Srebrenica massacred a group of woodcutters who were there cutting down the woods outside the enclave, and I have all their names. They were Serbs. Precisely by the members of the 28th Division. Do you remember that particular attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you could give me the area where this happened, it could refer to the action reported to me south of Zeleni Jadar, but in this way and with these details, it was not reported to me and so I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember these woodcutters and that it wasn't an attack at all on soldiers, although this wouldn't have been allowed in a protected area either, and that people were killed. You don't have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I said before, no, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Franken. You just mentioned the 28th Division, and it was in Srebrenica during the time you were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Originally it was all the 8th Operational Group but during the period I was there it was transferred into the 28th Muslim Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because a previous witness explained here that that 28th Division was established after Srebrenica was left, later on. But your testimony is that while you were there in Srebrenica itself, it came to be known as the 28th Division, transformed into the 28th Division; is that right, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that's correct. The fact that the name changed and the organisation changed was given to us by the staff of that 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you tell me, please, how many men that 28th Division numbered, in view of the fact that you're a soldier yourself. Could you give us some basic data about that 28th Division, the ones you consider important as a soldier yourself to get an idea of the general picture, the scope and manpower in that division.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I we estimated, because we didn't get the information from the Muslim side as well, there were 4 to 4.500 armed men. They were organised in four brigades with a staff who had two HQs, one in Potocari and one in Srebrenica. As I should estimate their combat power was pretty poor, not due to the number of men but to discipline and training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That they were poorly disciplined I assume is borne out by this piece of information, that there were a lot of internal clashes and conflicts, mutual killings and looting within the enclave itself and onslaughts on OPs of your battalion, and I assume you had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know of internal clashes and conflicts. I know of a brigade commander killing two of his men in the end phase because they were threatening one of our OPs, but looting I do not know. And onslaughts of OPs, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they attacked, the OPs? Were they attacked while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The OPs were attacked by the Bosnian Serb army in the end phase. Probably you're referring to one man -- one of my men killed by the Muslim division in the end phase. It concerns one of the members of the Observation Post Foxtrot which was attacked by the Bosnian Serb army, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 29010 to 29014. withdrew and on their way back to the next position engaged a Muslim roadblock where the gunner of the APC was shot by one of the Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Franken, you say that the Serbs were active there. The Serbs didn't kill a single one of your men, did they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If I said Serbs in this case, I mean Bosnian Serbs. They did not kill in the enclave. I had one casualty with one of my companies in another area, Simin Han, caused by Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you're not testifying about that. And regardless of the fact that you're not, was this your man and was that caused by something that the Bosnian Serbs did? Is that how that came about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you refer to the enclave area there, I did not have casualties as a consequence of Bosnian Serb action. As I told before, there was one casualty due to Bosnian Serb action but again in another area, Simin Han, Nasetna [phoen] front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that? Where did that happen? Where was your man a casualty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Was in the other Bosniak area, I'd say about 40 Ks, kilometres east of Tuzla. One of my companies had a mission over there, the same kind of mission we had in the enclave, and one of the members of that company was killed, as described before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who killed him? What happened, actually? Can you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. He was part of a crew of an observation post. The observation post was shelled by the Bosnian Serb army, and he died in that shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now tell me please, Mr. Franken, do you consider that the protected area regime was not respected since this 28th Division was there and that it launched skirmishes on territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska out from the area and killed people? I gave you two examples. One was the village of Visnjica and the massacre of the woodcutters. There were similar examples elsewhere, but was that the standard practice, that they would leave the zone and enter into these operations and crimes in the environment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Basically, the 28th Division could not exist because the area of Srebrenica should have been demilitarised and there should not have been any Bosniak military formations in there. In fact, that answers your question. If they are not supposed to be there, they're particularly not supposed to perform whatever action under the cover of the UN battalion being DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
