utterances.text: Well, in view of that fact, what you've just said, explain to me, please, how are you able to state that in the few first months that you spent in Srebrenica, and you say that in point 3 of your statement, that there were very few incidents worth mentioning. That's what you say. And that the humanitarian aspect was not catered to sufficiently because of lack of supplies. Now, was it worth mentioning what was going on and what you've just explained to us was going on? Wasn't that worth mentioning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Two things: You asked me whether the 28th Division had some legal basis to perform actions in Bosnian Serb area. I answered that. Secondly, what I stated there is on base of those incidents reported to me. I told you before that I got knowledge of two actions of the Muslim division outside the enclave. As far as I recollect, those would have been in April and May somewhere. So it's not a question of not worth mentioning. I didn't have any information, and the information I gave about actions I mentioned. And the fact that the humanitarian aspect was not catered to sufficiently because lack of supplies had much to do with the fact that the Bosnian Serbs had to grant the UN every transport of supplies every time the UNHCR wanted to do that. There was quite some harassment from that side, which meant that they didn't get enough supplies into the enclave, not only for the civil population but for the battalion as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you happen to recall, Mr. Franken, that for the most part what the UNHCR sent in, or the UN sent in, for humanitarian purposes and the requirements of UNPROFOR for the most part went via Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct. As far as that came further, the route normally was not through Serbia but directly through -- over the road through Zenica. So from the area of Sarajevo, from the logistics base there. There was a part coming from Zagreb and then through Serbia. And I should say in Serbia itself the problem -- there were no problems. The problems arose at the Serbian/Bosnian Serb border if we didn't have a clearance for a convoy like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have any problems through Serbia anywhere, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We seldom did. And as far as I know, UNHCR seldomly had problems crossing Serbia in the direction of Srebrenica or in the direction of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that the UNHCR never had any problems in Serbia, but we can leave that for another witness.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's why I said as far as I know, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Franken. Tell me, please, in view of the fact that you're a soldier, is it true that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, prior to the beginning of the summer in 1995, was a strong military force, I would say, and it was supported in terms of intelligence, materiel, and finances from outside. In 1995, it numbered some 270.000 men, if my figures are correct on the basis of what my associates have collected. There was six corps, 112 brigades, 45 independent battalions, and of course, tanks, APCs, artillery pieces, multiple-rocket launchers, et cetera. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Whether these exact figures are right, I can't remember. But in the preparation for my mission in 1995 we got information, of course, about the Bosnian -- Bosniak army as well, and it looked like a pretty well structured, organised military force. And whether they were supported in terms of intelligence, materiel and finances from the outside, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the support which even went partially through parts of UNPROFOR? You don't know anything about that support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. You must consider the fact that I was in an enclave, pretty isolated, on battalion level. So if you have a question like that, probably you'll have to go up ranking in the UN whether they knew. I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Franken. That's why I won't ask you anything else about that. But as Srebrenica itself and the activities of the Muslim forces out of the protected area, I assume we will agree it cannot be viewed in isolation from the general context. Do you know that the Muslim army had a plan of two stages which meant, with respect to Srebrenica, linking the enclaves of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I heard about a plan like that when I was back in Holland, which means after, say, in July 1995. I did not know of a plan like that during the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it part of the plan to gain control of the central Drina River valley? Was that part of the Muslims' plan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know the details of that plan. Only thing I knew, that there should have been a plan on the Muslim side to in fact relieve the enclaves and add them to the Muslim area generally said -- described as the Sarajevo-Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that this division that was in Srebrenica consisted of five brigades and mountain and police forces attached to them? According to the information I have collected, there were -- the 280th Brigade along the axis Potocari-Srebrenica, then the 281st Brigade Pobude-Cerska. 282nd Zeleni Jadar-Bojna-Srebrenica. 283rd, Podravno-Buje-Vigor; 284th, Ravni-Buljim-Milacevici-Potocari. And the Mountain Battalion and police forces that were deployed in Srebrenica, Potocari, Cerska, in the role of the reserve of the 28th Infantry Brigade. Are you familiar with this entire structure of forces that they had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The four brigades is according to knowledge I had, what you describe as the reserve of the 28th Infantry, probably division you mean, was -- it was known that Oric, being the commander of the 28th Division, had a more or less special unit at his own disposal. As far as we could see or observe, it was not organised in the battalion, for as far as police forces are concerned, well, he used them as some kind of personal instruments, but we never discovered a battalion structure in that group of men under the direct control of Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the five brigades that I have listed, and this battalion that you say was under Oric's direct control, according to my information, the total numerical strength was between 10 and 12.000 men. Is that figure correct, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The figure we dealt with was observations we did and observations DutchBat II, our predecessors did, and then we came to the amount of 4 -- max 4.500 armed men. In fact of course the 28th Division had all men at his disposal, but for my information or for my decision-making, it is important to know how many armed men he has, and that's what the figure of about 4.500 men. It is -- to me it is not very probable that they had 10 up to 12.000 armed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Franken. That is what you can tell us to the best of your knowledge, that he only had about 4.500 men in this small area. This is, after all, a respectable force, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a report dated the 28th of June, 1995 -- this was the time when it was necessary to strictly observe the safe area regime, I assume, because we're talking about the 28th of June, 1995, in a combat report 285th of the East Bosnian Light Brigade, the superior command, that is the 2nd Corps of the army of BH, is told that the brigade has infiltrated nine sabotage groups for committing sabotage in the rear of the army of Republika Srpska, and the commander is boasting that in those operations, 40 Chetniks, as he calls them, were killed. Do you know anything about those events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. We in general had a massive lack of intelligence, especially of everything concerning actions or events we could not see ourselves. We never had any reports from other units or from higher echelon, in fact, what happened, neither from the parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, Mr. Franken, to tell me whether apart from these forces of the 28th Infantry Division you had occasion to establish the existence of any paramilitary formations in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The problem was that the personnel of the 28th Division was not recognisable by a uniform or something. They had parts of uniforms. Later in May, some company-sized units had new combat suits. So whether there were between those half military dressed men paramilitary formations, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the men with weapons you considered to belong to the 28th Division, and you couldn't distinguish among them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I should make a remark about the men with weapons. They did some training but without the weapons because we -- if we got the opportunity, we still tried to demilitarise until a certain stage. And in fact, your statement that we considered all men operating in a military way to belong to the 28th Division, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the Drina Corps, at the beginning of July 1995, was confronted with the danger of the 2nd Muslim Corps from Tuzla making a breakthrough towards Srebrenica and them linking up with the forces of the 28th Division in Srebrenica and Zepa and thus cutting in half the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It could be, but as an assessment of the Drina Corps - and as you know I was part of DutchBat, not of the Drina Corps - this fact or this threat was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know anything at all about the activities of the 2nd Muslim Corps from Tuzla towards Srebrenica at the beginning of July and their preparations for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I did not. Again, we were enormously isolated, and not only geographically but for -- as information concerns, as well. We were more or less on an island over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand that. But those conflicts, did they start, as my information says, sometime around the 6th of July, 1995, in the morning when the enclave was narrowed down to the urban part of the town and when the activities of the Muslim army from Srebrenica against the Drina Corps were thwarted and prevented? Is that how things evolved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably you refer to the wish of the 28th Division to launch a counter-attack as opposing the Bosnian Serb attack in the area Zeleni Jadar. We advised them not to do so, and they followed our device -- sorry, they followed our advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then that the 28th Division combat structure started to fall apart?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, it became pretty clear that the -- as I mentioned before the lack of discipline and structure in that 28th Division. It became pretty clear, let's say, around the 9th of July, 10th of July, when there was an actual attack from the south in the direction of Srebrenica. Local commanders did not keep up to orders of the division, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then, Mr. Franken, that there was a breakthrough towards Tuzla and Kladanj by large parts of the 28th Division in groups of 1.000 or several hundred men under arms who were endeavouring to break through the ranks of the army of Republika Srpska and to get to Tuzla and Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as we know, we observed that there were no Muslim forces in the area any more in the morning of the 11th -- correction, morning of the 12th. We were not informed where they were. And around the 13th or 14th, we were informed that the 28th Division had performed a breakthrough to the Tuzla area out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it clear that this breakthrough by several thousand members of the 28th Division breaking its way towards Tuzla and Kladanj took place under fire? There was combat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then correct that a large number, since the whole breakthrough operation was taking place in conflict, that a large number of those men were killed in conflict, in combat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, on my side it's more or less speculation if I base it on the quality of the 28th Division, the number of armed men. The fact that the Bosnian Serb army had his defence lines around the enclave, they have to break through, and it's obvious that there should have been quite some casualties; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is no doubt that a large number, or quite a number, as you say, of them were killed in the fighting during that breakthrough. Is that right, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At least it is -- it's logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's logical for me, too, because I can only observe it on the basis of the data provided to me. Now, could you tell me, please, is it true, but you do say in paragraph 19 of your statement that the Operative Group of the division headquarters no longer had control over their soldiers. Is that right? They were in groups numbering 500 to 2.000 making their way through.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The first part of your statement is correct. I stated that they had no longer control over their soldiers, and I mean in the period, let's say 10th, 11th -- 10th, 11th of July, 9th, 10th, 11th of July. Whether they had control during the breakthrough or the planning of the breakthrough, I do not know because I didn't witness that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in the night of the 10th of July, 1995, you were still negotiating with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not with the army of the Bosnian Serbs? You refer to that in paragraph 21 of your statement, let me just remind you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then also true that instead of surrendering and acquiring the status of prisoners of war, the command of the 28th Division chose the worst possible solution for them in the military sense by ordering a breakthrough towards Kladanj and in combat order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Whether it was the worst possible solution, I do not know, but obviously they chose for the breakout, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the direction of their breakthrough, was it through Jaglici, Buljim, Pobude, Cerska, Snagovo, Crni Vrh, Negovici, Bajkovac, and Nezuk? Was that the direction, the route that they took in the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I heard about the details of the breakthrough when I was back in Holland. In general, I understood, that was the information I had then, they went up north. That means from the -- they should have been gathered in the Slatina area, that is on the west side, the wooded area on the west side of the enclave, and then due north. And going due north you meet Jaglici, et cetera, but for the rest of the route as told to me afterwards, I did not know at that moment what route they would take or were taking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But you just knew of this first point that I mentioned, but later I assume you established the direction they took. So would that correspond to what I just said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean that I knew that I knew there was a breakout performed by the 28th Division, yes. In that very moment I was told that they out north. That is part of the route I described to you before, and that's where my knowledge about that breakthrough ends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding their movement, I understand that your knowledge ends there, but do you know that wherever they could, they liquidated parts of the units of the Drina Corps, not just parts of combat units but also logistic units and civilians who they encountered along the way? Whatever they could destroy and kill on the Serb side, they did. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. I heard stories about it again when I was back in Holland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that at the time on the Muslim side there were very many casualties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I think I answered that question before. It is logical that there are quite an amount of casualties if you perform an action like that, but no figures were given to me or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it clear from this that a large number of the casualties that were victim of this armed conflict were later included in the number of victims that were allegedly executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, can you possibly answer a question like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So this is your account, is it; that the people who were in the mass graves at Srebrenica were people who were breaking out? Is that the -- is that the account we're to be asked to accept in due course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is for me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, not for you, for Mr. Milosevic who is putting these matters. Is this the story, so that we know what it is that your case is about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I do not have my version of events or my case. I am endeavouring to help in establishing the truth in connection with all those events in Srebrenica. I do not have my version. I wish I did, but I really do not. On the basis of what this witness is testifying, there is no doubt that there were large casualties within the 28th Division during combat operations. That is a fact that we have established. Now, what share they have in the total number of casualties, I cannot even assume now, but there is no doubt that there were very high casualties during the combat operations. I have no version of my own, Mr. May, nor could I have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were operations when they were breaking through an encirclement under combat. Later on you studied the question of Srebrenica even later when you came back to Holland. Did you know anything at all about something that is stated in an interview granted by Hakija Meholjic, president of the SDP of Srebrenica, in June 1998 in their newspaper Dani, as to how Izetbegovic called them to come to Sarajevo and how he asked them, "What do you think about the exchange of Srebrenica, giving Srebrenica in exchange for Vogosca?" And they rejected it. And then Hakija Meholjic is saying this, who is from Srebrenica, that apparently Izetbegovic told them, "You know, Clinton offered me, in April, 1993 after Cerska and Konjevic Polje had fallen, that the Chetnik forces could enter Srebrenica, massacre 5.000 Muslims, and then there would be a military intervention." Did you ever familiarise yourself with this strategy of Izetbegovic's when he relied on Clinton and this major tragedy in Srebrenica as a pretext for a military intervention? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, again I think it's important for me to emphasise that during that situation, during the events in Srebrenica, I was on battalion level, and yes, I read all kinds of stories when I was back in Holland in papers. I do not hope that you are going to ask me what I did read in papers. There was a hell of a lot because Holland was very concerned and very occupied with the Srebrenica question. So answering your question, I do not know anything about that more than any other civilian reading papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in view of the fact that you were in Srebrenica and followed the course of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop this. There is no point asking the witness, as he correctly points out, something that he's merely followed later on. I've allowed you some latitude to ask him questions about things which he'd read on his return, but you really must concentrate on the matters he can deal with himself. He can deal with what happened when he was there, but he can't deal with what he's read in the newspapers. It's not worth the evidence, it's not worth the time, something which somebody has read in a newspaper. So let's concentrate on the evidence which he can give.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. May, and I'm not asking Colonel Franken to talk about that, but this provocation of massive deaths among members of the 28th Division is beyond doubt, and it is also beyond doubt that all the victims in Srebrenica have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's all in dispute, and you're making a speech. You can make your speeches in due course. Now, time, as you know, with this witness is very much of the essence. Do you have more relevant questions for him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I do, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm -- I would like to make it easier for you, Mr. Franken, to find your way around in the answers, and I'm pointing to point 67 of your statement, to help you. Is it true that a certain number of males had already been taken away to that white house, as it was called, for interrogation and that you sent a military observer from the UN there to see whether people were being -- were disappearing, and he reported back to you and said that he had seen the same number of people enter the house and leave the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what he reported to me. That's about when he was about three hours in the beginning in the -- in or near the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And this running after members of the 28th Division that had dispersed around Srebrenica and fled in different directions in large armed groups, was that a legitimate and lawful military operation that cannot be classed amongst any kind of incriminated action -- classed as incriminated action of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's hardly to judge for me concerning the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right, Colonel. There's no need for you to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, on that night of the 10th of July when a meeting was held between the lieutenant colonel, I think he was, Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, and the civilian and military authorities in the enclave, at that same night at the marketplace in Srebrenica, there were another 1.500 men in uniforms and armed. And that is in paragraph 86 of your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is the number that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans estimated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the remainder was already on its way through the woods and forests, attempting to break through?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: More or less speculation. They were not at the moment not in sight of Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remind the Chamber that there's the video that's available at any time. It will be about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm pointing out paragraph 86. Did you order -- issue an order for the defence of Srebrenica and the next day you didn't see a single BH soldier? "The following morning, we could not see a single BH soldier," you say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I issued the order for the defence of Srebrenica, as I recall, on the evening of the 9th, and when we missed, so to say, the 28th Division was in the morning of the 12th. Correct: Morning of the 11th, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when what you say in paragraph 86 was it that you didn't see a single BH soldier? When was that? The following morning, you say. What date was that, that following morning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was after the colonel saw on the 10th those 1.500 men, and the next day the mass of them were disappeared. That's why I said the morning of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the morning of the 11th they weren't there any more. And is it true that you heard that the BH soldiers were gathering to the east of Slatina and the Buljinska ravine - and according to my information, that is a very wooded and steep area - precisely in order to break through towards Tuzla. And that's what you say in paragraph 86 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, only that came not to my knowledge on the morning of the 11th already. That was later. We were just puzzled where they were, and we didn't have any idea what they were doing or known with the fact that they were planning or performing a breakthrough at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me just read the last sentence in paragraph 86: "I also heard that the BH army had suffered great casualties on an attack on the eastern flank of the BSA positions." That's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Great losses were sustained.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact, what was going on was an attack of parts of the 28th Division on that eastern flank of the positions of the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know details like that. Again, the only thing I heard, and again it was not military intelligence or information but there were a hell of a lot of rumours, so from the -- from all sides I heard the rumour that they were gathering, et cetera, what I declared before or what I stated before. Whether they were going on on an attack, what kind of a flank of the army of the BSA, I do not know. Again, my knowledge stops at the fact that they were gone and later on I heard rumours that they were performing a breakthrough. The actual fact that it took place came to my knowledge somewhere around 13th or 14th by information of Colonel Jankovic who reported me that he had -- they had made that again -- sorry, I correct myself. That the Muslim forces were trying to break through and they made about 6.000 POWs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've just mentioned that, although I didn't notice it in reading through the material, although I do have a lot of material to get through, that's true, so I might have missed that part. But when Mr. Nice presented his summary of your statement a moment ago -- but tell me, who is Colonel Jankovic? You've mentioned him. Who was Colonel Jankovic? What position did he hold or function perform?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was presented to me as the colonel in charge of the withdrawal of DutchBat, and anything about the withdrawal I had to coordinate with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know what position he held except for being in charge of your withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. His normal position was not known to me. I asked him for it, but he didn't give an answer. Later, I learned that he was in the intelligence department of the Drina Corps, but that is later on when I was back in Holland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Franken. So I've just heard in the summary presented a moment ago by Mr. Nice that Colonel Jankovic quite simply, and I didn't believe my ears when I heard it, whether I had heard correctly or whether that is what it actually says in your statements, that, "Colonel Jankovic informed me that they had 6.000 prisoners of war and that they would be killed." Now, this man Colonel Jankovic, did he actually say that those prisoners of war would be killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I neither recollect that hearing in the summary of Mr. Nice, but he did not explain to me that they would be killed. He told me that they had 6.000 POWs, prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I never said that in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This will be a convenient moment to consider the rest of this case, the rest of this case as far as the witness's evidence is concerned. The accused has had very nearly the allotted time. We will consider what extra time he should have, and you want to play your videos. It might be a convenient moment to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please, and we do indeed have another witness, of course, here who has been inconvenienced for various reasons many times before and we would be anxious to start him today if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi. Examined by Mr. Waespi: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next portion of the segment could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what you see here are our trucks coming from the Srebrenica area arriving on the Potocari HQ. In that phase, we originally were trying to evacuate the civil hospital in Srebrenica, but we did initially not succeed because refugees overwhelmed our vehicles, and as you see, hung on it. So we brought them away and then later, after some terms of transports like that we succeeded in evacuating the casualties from the hospital Srebrenica. What you see here is the unloading of the people from those trucks. This is at the HQ of DutchBat Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient means in terms of medication, food, water for these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. You should consider that the temperature was about 30, 35 degrees Celsius. It was very hot. I had food supplies for two days for the battalion, which means 400 men, and I had the maximum of water I could produce because the whole water system in the enclave didn't function. We had to purify it ourselves at 7.000 litres per day. If you understand under those circumstances, humidity, et cetera, that a normal not working man in good condition needs up to five, up to seven litres of water a day, then you can imagine with 30.000 in bad shape, being civilians, I did not have water. One of our arguments to not -- not to make a military stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks a lot. If we could move on, and please comment on what we are seeing now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here is a recording of the first meeting between Colonel Karremans, the man in the back with the grey moustache, with Mladic. On the left side you see Colonel Jankovic, on the back left General Mladic, and on the right side the civilian is Petar, the interpreter I described to you before. Mladic now is bullying Colonel Karremans about the fact that we shot at him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are preparing the next clip. It usually takes some time. Can you tell us who was present from the Dutch side apart from Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That first meeting, my two liaison officers, being NCO named Rave and Major Boering was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the next portion we're going to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic. Due to the text, this is recording of the second meeting on that evening. Then on our side Colonel Karremans, our liaison again, and three representatives of the civilian population, which we had to organise pretty quickly, were there and as far as we can see to it, what he's saying, Mladic is addressing them now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one comment to make, Mr. May, in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's play this and then we'll have comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it refers to this clip. Mladic isn't saying "opstati" but -- to survive, but to stay. He has misspoken and made a slip of the tongue. He says "opstati" instead of "ostati," and then puts himself right, to remain there, meaning to remain in Srebrenica or to leave Srebrenica, and not to survive, and the translation was "survive," that's the word used, whereas he corrects himself and says to remain. "Opstati," "ostati." You can take a translator or interpreter and they'll be able to bear out what I say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Mandic, one of the three representatives, on his left and for the viewers on the right side, Major Boering, then to the left Major Karremans, Petar the interpreter, Colonel Jankovic, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are waiting for the third clip. In this connection it's the meeting on the next day, on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see Mr. Nuhanovic, one of the three representatives of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we hear the soundtrack as well, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then seeing in front Mladic, to the left Krstic, then the civilian Petar next to him, Colonel Karremans -- then-Colonel Karremans I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And now we're moving on to the next clip, and that's 12th of July in Potocari and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see here a situation partly out of our HQ where the area of the bus station, which you have seen on the map before, we gathered about 25.000 of people, and we had about 5.000 on our compound, on our base. We tried -- you see a red and white tape, and which we used as the boundary of the area where the refugees were concentrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you have seen General Mladic in that area giving a TV interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not personally. It was reported to me but later on I saw a TV recording of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, how many more of these do you have? How much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It will be about five more. Unfortunately, there is always about 20 seconds to 30 seconds in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll play this one and then we'll break because we've gone beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you see the procedure, or the consequence of the procedure of separating the men on the other side of the buses and trucks. The women and children were brought to there, you can see them there. And these are the men probably led to the well-known white house. This is the other side of the row of the buses where women and children are going to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen's separate opinion is available; paragraph 3, 17 to 20, and 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the next clip segment could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you saw there was a multiple-launch rocket system that the Bosnian Serbs used in shelling Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the recording of the interior of one of the evacuation buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now we have three clips left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime, how many Dutch troops were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In total I had about 310 men, but a major part of them were not combat soldiers, sir. I had about 147, 150 combat-trained soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see is one of our surgeons, Colonel Kramer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his function?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was one of our surgeons of the mobile hospital we had in the enclave, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll see an UNMO in the next frame. Can you tell us what the UNMOs were doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Major, as I recall him, Kingori. He was one of the two UNMOs stationed in the Srebrenica area, and he is one of the UNMOs I positioned near the white house to control what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again to remind us what happened at the white house.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The interrogation, the first interrogation of the men after they were separated from their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we see a last clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see here is the road to the white house, and what you see is, next to the goat, packs and bags taken from the men. Later on, they were burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the balcony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: This is the balcony of the white house where a couple of the men already with or waiting for their first questioning by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That concludes the video part, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in one of the clips, we saw Mr. Mladic saying, "You can either disappear or survive." Earlier, you said that Mladic had spoken and had corrected himself. Was it in relation to a similar sentiment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw on the first clip at the first meeting when Mladic says either "ops --" he goes halfway into the word and then he changes it to "ostati or nestati," which means "remain or disappear." That was the first clip. And the next time he when receives them, he did say "ostati or nestati," which means to survive, to prevail, or to disappear. I don't know if you understand me, Mr. Robinson. But this is quite visible. The first time he made a slip of the tongue and corrected himself, but on the second occasion he does say "ostati or nestati."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered the time you should have. We've decided 20 minutes more for you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have to object. You said that time was of the essence. That is a fundamental difference between us, because I think that the truth should be of the essence and not time. I haven't asked a single irrelevant question of Mr. Franken now for you to be able to caution me. I am unable to cross-examine him in 20 minutes. You can cut short, that is your right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have not challenged, I don't think, any of his evidence at all. It's true that I haven't stopped you because you get some latitude, but all the questions you've asked have to do with the Bosnians, as far as I can see, nothing about the Serbs. You may like to ask some questions about that in the 20 minutes remaining. That is one of the things that we consider when we consider the time you should have available. If you use it to put forward counter-arguments the whole time, that's a matter which we consider. Now, if you have anything to challenge in this officer's evidence, you should challenge it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that Mr. Franken is speaking to the best of his knowledge about events and facts, and I am endeavouring to place that within the context of the allegations which the side opposite is endeavouring to construe. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as not to waste time, Mr. Franken, let us make a small digression as we have just been viewing these TV clips. The first meeting between Mladic and Colonel Karremans, it is given in tab number 4. I don't want us to play that once again, just tell me, was it Mladic who asked for the meeting or was it Karremans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: During the end phase, we repeatedly request liaison to the Serb side. As I recollect, the place and time of meeting with the Serbs was brought to us by -- by -- through OP -- our Observation Post Papa who was at the entrance of the enclave, and the first meeting Colonel Karremans tried to postpone that but it was commanded at the time as it took place, as I recollect correctly, it was 2000 hours that evening, and he was surprised to meet Mladic there, because he thought he would meet somebody else there. So it is not exactly to be pointed whether it was on our request or on the request of the Bosnian Serbs. It could be a reply to our former requests, but I do not know. It was established through Papa where it was said a meeting 2000 hours in the hotel in Bratunac. That's how it came to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I remember, Mladic says, "You asked to see me, here I am," or something to that effect. So I gathered from that that Karremans had requested the meeting. Is it true that at that meeting Mr. Karremans said that he had been in touch with the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is requesting that the population be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do not recollect a text like that. I know that Mr. Colonel Karremans expressed his concerns about the situation of the operation and asked, that was at least his intention as he left the camp, and asked about supplies, et cetera, et cetera, and other things, the humanitarian situation concerning. I do not know whether this tape covers the complete meeting. I suppose it doesn't so -- I only was debriefed about that meeting. I was not present, so I don't know exactly what who said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I hope we can check that by viewing the whole tape. And as far as I was able to see, Karremans says that he was in touch with the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is requesting that the population be moved out. But that can be checked. In paragraph 70 of your statement, you say that on only two occasions you heard about alleged executions and that a soldier from Company C had seen members of the Bosnian Serb army killing one man. And in another case, Lieutenants Koster and Rutten found the bodies of nine men. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that there were armed conflicts with the army of Republika Srpska on the road from Bratunac towards Konjevici? And there were a large number of casualties along that road. You have that in your examination of the hearing, the parliamentary inquiry. This is paragraph 35, I think. Otherwise, it is on page 5 of that document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is true. That was reported to me by the first escort teams who were able to return to the HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. None of your soldiers saw an execution anywhere, and if they had seen it you would have been informed about it. So I link this to the paragraph from this document I referred to, Royal Netherlands Army Srebrenica debriefing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I said before that I heard about alleged executions, but the C Company soldiers saw actually an execution, and the nine bodies found by the Lieutenants Koster and Rutten were actually there. From my other teams, I did not get any reports about actual executions. The returning escort teams reported to me that alongside the road -- and you said Konjevici, I suppose you mean the road from Bratunac in the direction of Vlasenica -- they saw there a pretty large number of casualties, of dead men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the conflict occurred with the army of Republika Srpska, along that route; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, do you know that on Monday the 10th of July, the commander of the observation post received orders to coordinate with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that that evening a conflict broke out among BH soldiers upon which there were dead and wounded? I draw your attention to this that you refer to in the debriefing document on page 37. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose you refer to the Observation Post Mike. Mike in its original position was under heavy shelling by the Bosnian Serb army and got permission to withdraw about 400 metres. Doing that, they were stopped by local Bosniak soldiers who threatened them with an anti-tank weapon. The brigade commander of that north -- of that brigade of the Bosnian army interfered and that resulted in his -- him shooting these two men, threatening the OP crew and their APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say - this is on page 37, 358 - "Around midday there was chaos among the soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and internal fighting started again amongst them." Was there fighting amongst themselves at the time? This is in your debriefing document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, I suppose this -- or this refers to the situation at OP Mike. The fighting with guns in between them, there was quite a lot of quarreling and fighting between them at other OPs as well, whether they would allow us not or -- not to or to -- what do you call it -- take other positions with our APCs. The only moment that there was reported to me fighting in the sense of firing guns at each other was the situation in the area of OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that there were abuses of UN uniforms? Do you know that soldiers of the BH army, fully clothed in blue berets and blue caps came 15 metres close to an OP and, acting as UN members, opened fire on the army of Republika Srpska, so it appeared as if the UN had opened fire on them. Is that correct, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Both parties used our uniforms, not only in the end phase but even in the period before the end phase. The Bosniaks had a habit in trying to attract fire to OP locations by taking positions quite close to our OPs and then firing at the Bosnian Serb army; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did they get your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking how did they get the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They got our uniforms by probably the OPs who were left or overridden by the Serbs. There was quite a lot of equipment left over. And where they were dressed completely in uniforms, probably they came out of the abandoned compound base of B Company based in Srebrenica, because of course you can understand, we were not able to take everything along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, please, point 413 on page 45 of your debriefing. It says literally: "Soldiers of the BH army fully clothed and with blue berets, or blue caps, came 15 metres to -- close to our OP. They opened fire from this position in the direction of the front line of the army of Republika Srpska so that it appeared as if the UN had opened fire. In this way, they endeavoured to attract fire from the army of Republika Srpska to the observation post and in that way to draw the Dutch Battalion into the combat activities." This is in the minutes of your debriefing. It is contained there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I'm not denying that. I'm just trying to get several events in a time frame. As it stands there, as it is testified by me as you refer to, it is correct. No doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since it is well-known that nine Bosnian men were killed in Potocari in the night between the 12th and 13th of July - this is on page 48 of the debriefing - is it known also that it was unestablished, that it remained unclear, whether the mentioned Bosnian Serbs could be considered perpetrators because a soldier of the Dutch Battalion heard from locals that the killing occurred because of a quarrel among the locals. And you say literally: "It remained open whether the Bosnian Serbs can be considered to be the perpetrators because a soldier of the DutchBat heard from the local population that the killing took place because of a quarrel among the locals. The DutchBat was not allowed to remove the bodies." Is that correct, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to read back your question, sir. Just hold -- that is correct. It remained open because we didn't have actual proof that the Bosnian Serbs did that. It is -- the rumour was that it was an internal quarrel, but if you look to the location where it took place, if you see that day, nine bodies were in a row all shot the same way, it's very, very unlikely -- and as I say, I can't prove it, but it's very unlikely that any Muslims were involved in that seeing the time that it happened. In that period, 12 or 13th of July, we were not in control but the Bosniaks absolutely were not in control as well. And if I say in a former statement it remained open, yes, I mean to say we could not prove or we did not prove that the Bosnian Serbs actually did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the contrary. I was just quoting from your debriefing in which it says that it occurred because of a quarrel among the local population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with it. There's no need to repeat what you've said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that two soldiers of the Dutch Battalion declared that they saw 500 to 700 bodies on their return from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac on the 14th of July? This is on page 51 of the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That would be the crew of OP Alpha, which has been in position until the very end, and I know that they have declared -- I read it myself, that they reported bodies, not these numbers, but bodies of which 40 or 50 loaded on a truck alongside that road. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally, the fall of Srebrenica, massive losses, civilian casualties, everything that happened over there, I believe, was an introduction to NATO military airstrikes. Wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't judge whether that was the only cause, but I know that one of the reasons that NATO interfered was the situation Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After establishing control over Srebrenica on the 11th of July, did the army of Republika Srpska take measures to ensure controlled evacuation of all those who wished to go and that this should be carried out accompanied with necessary security measures?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If they did, I couldn't observe them, and the measures we tried to take, and I mean escorting the convoys, were, as I told you before, massively harassed and prevented by -- by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that for the evacuation of the civilian population the special secretary of the Secretary-General Yasushi Akashi asked that this be done on the 11th of July, a day before the beginning of the evacuation, and he sent a telegram to you at headquarters presenting his own suggestions. Achieve agreement with the army of Republika Srpska to allow the population to go to Tuzla, and secondly, that the convoys to Tuzla be escorted by UN personnel. You are aware of that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and it's not different from what I said before. We tried to escort them by UN personnel, being DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we have this in mind, that is the United Nations' position, surely it is clear that the thesis that the army of Republika Srpska had in a planned and organised manner evacuated the population from Srebrenica within the framework of any plan -- cleansing plan of its own does not stand. The evacuation was part of the UN plan and not of the army of Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that it is clear, but that would be a discussion. I -- in the statements you have from me, I already explained why I think it was organised and why it was prepared, and saying that the -- the fact that the UN by Mr. Akashi sends us a telegram that he knows, or the population is allowed to go to Tuzla, et cetera, to me it's no proof that it is clear that the BSA did not plan this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to give you another ten minutes, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Tapuskovic can then have ten minutes, and we then must start the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 11th of July, when they met at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, that is Karremans and Mladic, that Mladic stated that he did not intend to attack UN personnel and that the evacuation must be done on a voluntary basis? Is that right, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I remember it, his intention not to attack UN personnel, he used that in his -- I'm looking for a word -- when he accused Colonel Karremans of shooting at his personnel. And he, as I remember out of my debrief, he proposed a voluntary basis evacuation because he gave the choice, you can stay or go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what it says, too, in paragraph 43 of your statement, that the evacuation must be on a voluntary basis. That is what Mladic said. And I quote: "Mladic said the evacuation must be on a voluntary basis. He wanted to talk to the civilian and military leadership of the enclave." Is it true that Mladic was angry because the leaders of the BH army were not present? That is also stated in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's what I heard from Colonel Karremans, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say that during the evacuation the International Red Cross and other organisations would be present?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That again what I heard from my debrief from Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume Colonel Karremans was telling you the truth. And is it true that Mladic said that first the wounded, the elderly, women and children should be evacuated as well as members of the Dutch Battalion and that Karremans -- but Karremans did not agree with that -- wait a moment. Let me just look at paragraph 62 of your debriefing. Mladic said who should be evacuated first. This is on page 7, paragraph 4, of your statement. "The wounded, the elderly, women and children, men and members of the Dutch Battalion. Karremans did not agree with that."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it is as I stated then, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mladic say that the refugees would be taken in the direction of Kladanj and that it was agreed that you would escort the refugee columns, convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I -- as I recollect it, Mladic said that they could go anywhere they wanted. The Kladanj area was commanded, so to say, as far as I recollect the next day, and it was agreed that we would escort the refugee columns. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what Mladic really said, page 0092495. This is what I received from the side opposite. I think it is tab 2. He said he asked for absolute cooperation. "The aim is not the civilian Muslim population. I want to help you even though you don't deserve it, as a man and as an officer, but I will do it for those children of UNPROFOR --" he means the UNPROFOR soldiers -- "because I don't want their mothers to see them in coffins. I want to help the Muslim civilian population which is not to blame for what has happened, and that is why I would like to ask you the following: Are you capable of bringing here representatives of the civilian population? I would come to an agreement with them. You can leave from here, all of you, or all of you may stay or all of you may die. I don't want you to die. That is what was left out. I don't want you to die," he says. This was -- this is a transcript of the Karremans-Mladic meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Prosecution indicates the page number of the English transcript. While I'm waiting for the response, I have to note this for the record that the passage the accused has referred to earlier, that -- when he said -- when he asked the witness whether BH government requested a withdrawal of refugees, it appears on the page ending -- on page ending with the number 415 in the English transcript, and it is written that it is not the BH government but BH command that requested such a withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. We'll still try and find the other reference. We haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go on, Mr. Milosevic, while we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon, but let me say before that, Mladic says - Mladic therefore is speaking - and he says to Karremans, "You, Mr. Lieutenant Colonel, were duty bound in conformity with the agreement to disarm the Muslims in Srebrenica, whereas you armed them and were preparing them to go against the Serbs and you issued orders to your troops to fire against my soldiers. Let me hear what you want." And his response was: "If I can say so, they asked the BH forces from the enclave during last month to give them, to supply them weapons from points ..." and then there's three dots. This isn't included in the transcript. "... pieces of weapons." And then Karremans says: "Yes, two combat tanks, several mortars," and so on, but I don't have time to go into that in its entirety. Anyway, the point of all this is, and the passage you can't find, he says, and I'll repeat the last sentence: "You can all leave, all stay, or all die, and I do not wish you to die." That's what he says. And then several pages later on, and it is L0092511, those are the ERN numbers for me, on my copy, there is a discussion going on on behalf of a delegation of the population. Camila is speaking, and then Mladic, and he says: "It is your choice if you want to go. I'm not going to influence you. I don't mind anybody who is not to blame or innocent. So you can choose whether you want to go east via Serbia or into Serbia. I don't mind. If you want to go to the west, then you can state your views. You can tell us where you want to go." So that is what Mladic says, and this is in the transcript with respect to this departure, their leaving or not. And you have confirmed that in your own statement when you say the wounded, elderly, women and children, and then men and members of the battalion, et cetera, and then the last passage that I quoted. So I assume you are well aware of all that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Is it clear that the manner in which the Muslim population was to be transported from Potocari and other areas and the handover of weapons of this 28th Division was agreed at a meeting in Bratunac on the 11th and 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was, as far as I know, a proposal that the population was transported away from this area to any area of choice, as you stated yourself before. The handover of weapons of the 28th Division was not agreed upon, was a demand of Mladic, as far as I was debriefed by my CO, and my CO answered that we didn't have any contact with the 28th Division any more and we did not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That leaves many questions that I haven't been able to ask, and this man was a witness there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But anyway, Mr. Franken, do you know that in the last part of the main report of the Dutch government 2001 in point 10 it says literally, "There are no indications that the action was launched in cooperation with Belgrade either in respect of political or military coordination." Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I've read that, yes. I've read that, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in keeping with what you know from that period of time? Does it coincide with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At least for me, I did not have any evidence that it was launched in cooperation with Belgrade. And again, I read all kinds of reports and opinions and papers where all kinds of scenarios were analysed, et cetera. Again, I do not have any proof that the action, being the attack on the enclave, was launched in cooperation with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Ms. Wee for finding the first reference; Exhibit 592, tab 2, page 0092426, and it's at the foot of that page. I haven't found the last reference yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the Court's indulgence, may I get through one topic? I don't think it will take me more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Blagojevic case, testimony was used by Mr. Franken, and he was shown some passages from his report to the parliamentary commission with respect to the Srebrenica investigation, the lower house of the parliament in The Hague, a parliamentary inquiry on Srebrenica in the lower house, and an officer who was one of Mr. Franken's subordinates. May I ask Mr. Franken one thing first. I have photocopies for Their Honours, but you've already spoken about this. "Our predecessors told us that the zone hasn't been demilitarised when we assumed our duty and took over from the DutchBat. We were told that there were about 4 to 5.000 artillery pieces [as interpreted] in the enclave along with the men to go with it." Yes or no, words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The word "artillery pieces" is incorrect. 4 to 5.000 small arms, armed men in the enclave, that would be correct. Even now, 4 to 5.000 artillery pieces is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's how I understood it. That's what it says in your report. Small arms. I didn't say "artillery pieces." And then you said something else later on, and I think you'll remember, that information had arrived according to which a mysterious aeroplane landed at the airport, very strangely, and that after that you saw BH army soldiers being better armed and all of them had Kalashnikovs, and that you characterised all that as being very strange. I think "strange" is the word you used.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's what I stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you couldn't prevent it, and OP Delta was on that section of the road and when we heard about this transport, they changed their route, and then you could not do anything to prevent the arms from coming in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That supposes that these uniforms and new Kalashnikovs came in by what we call the pony express. OP Delta and Kilo were two observation points in the southern part of the enclave we established especially to have control of the Muslims in the southern direction. The point was that we were controlling the original routes, but, yeah, well, threatens to be a long story, but our OPs --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't think the rest of that is that essential. All I was asking you is that you weren't able to prevent the convoy with the arms passing by that way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that one of the tasks of the Dutch Battalion was to supervise and see that no side passes the separation line, crosses the separation line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had to supervise the confrontation line; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say, "What we did is we reported everything we saw. This referred to fire from small arms and others -- in the enclave during the night, and we -- the conclusion we made was that it was the Muslims coming out again."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was on one occasion, and that refers to the reported Bosnia attack in the north, but in general it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you go on to state the following: "Many blue berets had the feeling that the Muslims did not want to have their protection there and that they -- they were using the presence of the Dutch Battalion to engage in prohibited military activity." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the next portion right? You say that at the beginning of your statement: "According to our rules of engagement, if we were to be attacked, according to the principle of self-protection and defence with respect to non-combatants, they could use our armed systems." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I should like to ask you, and we're coming up to the 9th of July, and you say the following in that same statement of yours, that on the 9th of July, an order was issued to take preventive positions, assume preventive positions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Of course I don't know the literal -- literally text, but I look on the date. It is probably the order to defence the city of Srebrenica, and that is not preventive positions but blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those blockades were set up by you and your staff, as you say. You issued the order to Bravo, to Captain Groen, to Bravo Company, Captain Groen, and then you elaborated that plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it came to actually who was in command of the battalion, you said it was the operations centre, right, or operative centre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Of course in command of the battalion was the commanding officer. We had a division of tasks that -- which meant that I led operations in between the guidelines given by the CO. The operations room is just an analysing and information collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the parliamentary inquiry, you said that a great portion of the staff of the battalion was in Zagreb and that the head of the operation itself was in Zagreb, too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's right, and it should be chief operations, but that's a detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the Blagojevic case, a witness was heard, van Duijn, who was subordinate to Mr. Franken during those days. He was also questioned as a witness, and in that case as a Defence material, Mr. Van Duijn's statement was used and it was disclosed to us pursuant to Rule 68 exculpatory material, and it was introduced into evidence in that case, but not everything was explained on this subject matter. So I have to ask Mr. Franken a few more questions in view of what he did over there to see whether they were things that Mr. Franken knew about and whether what was done was done under his leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the parliamentary inquiry and the statement before it, mention is made of the fact that General Janvier's corps in Zagreb proposed the setting up of these blockades. Is that right? Or barriers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, but those positions already existed in some contingency plans we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van Duijn also said the following: "That order was issued as a green one." You know what a green order means.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I myself gave it the type, a green order. What was meant by that, we were there as blue berets only deterring military hostile action and using the weapons in self-defence. The very moment that I got orders to defend a city with the means I had, it would mean that the weapons are to be used not only in self-defence but in order to apply to the order, defend Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, I don't know whether you know about this, but Mr. Van Duijn in the report said that the order was like this: "If fire was opened at us, we are allowed to respond. First of all, shooting above their heads, the Serb heads, and then later on directly at them. This was, of course, part of the combat order by Captain Groen or, rather, it was a green order --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be an interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mystified as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What was the relevance of this, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the next question will show you why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just can you explain. If I ask a question, would you be courteous enough to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Because it is in that investigation, after what Mr. Groen said, and he lost his job and an investigation was conducted into the matter because he said, he said that the object of those barricaded positions was to attract fire to them from the positions of the Bosnian Serbs, thereby to incite air support. He wasn't conscious of that, but then he says, "Later on I came to realise that that's what it was all about, that the Serbs were being shot at and they were on the slopes of the various mountains in order to bring about air attacks, airstrikes." So is that what you understood as being the purpose of setting up these barriers or whatever? Because you weren't camouflaged. A green order means that you were to act from a shelter or behind a barrier and that you tried to do so as the witness says. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At first my order was to defend a city, and later on we heard that the strategic idea, or in Zagreb at HQ UNPROFOR was to attract fire from the blocking positions, so airstrikes could have been allowed is not an element in decision-making on 10/11, at that moment. So normally we -- what I -- again what I tried to explain to Captain Groen is that he was, if necessary, by use of all his weapons systems, to stop the Bosnian Serb army on the southern edge of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But don't you know that van Duijn issued an order that the Serbs should be shot at precisely at the moment when he saw them somewhere far off on the mountain slopes? The artillery was at 10 to 15 kilometres away, and van Duijn states that precisely. The people were on the tops of mountain slopes and that's when the order to shoot was given, and they did shoot. And that's what Mr. van Duijn says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very slow to object but I really must protest. I simply fail to follow the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this must be the last question. Perhaps you could answer, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. Mr. van Duijn repeated an order I gave, but there was no reaction time on that Serb infantry before they entered the city. And when I have dismounted infantry in a city, I have a major military problem. To be short, the only thing we could do is try to, by firing, prevent them from entering the city. I think I can keep it to this otherwise I'll get very tactical and military technical, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Five questions only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We really are so short of time. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladic's ultimatums that we've seen on the video, what did that show about his level of control?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but you gave me the right to ask one more question, I believe. Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've had a quarter of an hour. We really must -- this case must move along. What is your final question? What is the question? What is the question, so we can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several days prior to that, the Muslim side killed a Dutch soldier and nothing was -- no steps were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following: In all this when the Serbs were approaching the positions from which they were fired at, was anybody wounded on the DutchBat side, whereas they were being shot at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Shortly before my position Bravo 1 Bravo was shot at by a Serb tank and I had four injured on that position and I had to leave that position to another place. That's one. Secondly, yes, Muslim side killed one of my soldiers. Problem was that then my orders were still in the UN mandate and I was only to use my weapon systems in self-defence. The order to defend the city of Srebrenica was a normally military order, and in fact theoretically we could throw away our blue berets, put on our red berets, and start a fight. That's the difference, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Mladic's ultimatums, what do they show about his level of control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
