utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I'm thinking. Once in awhile I do. Well, in fact he was Supreme Commander, so it does not mean that -- no, it does not show that he was locally in tactical control, but it shows that he was in operational control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Akashi recommended evacuation. What was the reason, risk or threat that led to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I think both, and risk for the -- in the sense of the humanitarian situation. And threat, well, we had those threats of General Mladic and he showed that he was very willing to practice them in former locations, for instance, the shelling of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused suggested that the proper course would have been for people to have surrendered and become prisoners of war rather than to break out. Did those who broke out survive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, a part of them, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those who would have stayed as prisoners of war survive, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Stealing of APCs and clothes from your battalion, was this evenhanded as between Muslims and Serbs or did one side do this much more than the other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We never had thefts of APCs by the Muslims. In the end phase, it is possible that Muslims got hold of some of our uniforms, as I said before, by the remnants of the OPs formerly attacked by the BSA. The only ones who had -- stole APCs and jeeps from us were the Bosnian Serb army, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you've been asked a number of questions about what you've read, accounts given. Have you ever read any explanation from Mladic himself advanced as to the disappearance of these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll sit until 2.00, if that's of any assistance to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It certainly is. May he be brought in immediately by the usher. The next witness, please. He's protected and therefore we need the blinds down. Perhaps while the -- could we go into private session while the blinds come down and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to call Witness B-1524, with the permission of the Chamber

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: As Your Honours are aware, this witness has protective measures and he's also a 92 bis witness. So as soon as he's in, if we could perhaps exhibit his bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get a number for the package now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next Exhibit number is 595.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Could Witness 1524 kindly be shown his pseudonym sheet, which Your Honours will find at tab 1. Examined by Mr. Agha:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 1524, can you kindly look at the sheet and confirm that that is your name on the sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 1524, it's correct that you gave a statement before the Office of the Prosecution, which has subsequently been certified by the Registry. Could you kindly look at the statement in front of you and confirm that that is in fact your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, since Witness 1524 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: -- is a 92 bis witness, although I've prepared quite a detailed summary, due to the shortage of time, what I propose to do is just touch upon the real highlights of that. So in essence, the witness's summary is that he was a Serb who was born in Serbia and had been living in Zvornik for the past 20 years. He had good relations with both the Serbian and Muslim communities, so on the suggestion of the SDA, he was asked to join the SDS in order to try and make sure things went smoothly. At the first meeting he attended, which was headed by Mr. Brano Grujic who was president of the SDS, and the other cream of the Zvornik municipality, he left, saying that he did not want to be in the company of extremists and thieves and associated with Grujic. He left the meeting. In about February of 1992, he was again called by the SDS leadership to the military headquarters in Celopek. Present at that meeting were two regular JNA officers from Tuzla. One was a captain and the other was Lieutenant Sekanic who became in charge of a tank unit in Celopek. There were also 20 to 30 other JNA officers present. At this meeting, the object was to form a Serbian Zvornik Brigade. The Serbs were organised by the JNA where the SDA had to be organised by their local leadership. The witness was put in command of approximately 690 TO soldiers. At that meeting, the witness asked what the objectives of the brigade was. He was told that it was to defend against any attack from the Muslims, but if things turned out differently, it was none of his business. The witness asked Grujic what would happen to those Serbs who remained in Zvornik. Grujic told him that if they did not move out, then they would also be killed when the Serbs attacked. The witness came to learn there was a large stock of military weapons and mortars in Mali Zvornik which had come from the military depot at Bubanj Potok in Belgrade. After the meeting the SDS organised the distribution of weapons to the local Serbs through the managers of businesses, factories, and municipal organs. Indeed, many Serb families left Zvornik in anticipation of the oncoming hostilities. The SDA tried to encourage the witness to rejoin the SDS to protect their interests. The witness agreed to do so, and on the way into the headquarters saw at a checkpoint that there were armed men who were dressed similarly, spoke in Belgrade accents, and were greeted by the others there. He was told at the checkpoint that these were Arkan's men, whilst the men in the jeep belonged to a paramilitary group known as Mirko Jovic's group. At that point the witness realised that he could not go and join the Serbian TO because he knew that he'd have to kill people, and he would have no control over this. On 8th of April, small-arms fire commenced in Zvornik. The witness crossed over into Mali Zvornik where heavy shelling started from Mali Zvornik in Serbia into Zvornik. The next morning, the witness observed a Serbian flag flying from the main mosque in Zvornik with Serbian music being played from its minarets. It is now that the cleansing of the town started, that is, the killing of the male inhabitants. The witness could clearly see on the other side of the Drina armed soldiers wearing black uniforms entering apartments, some of whom he later heard had killed many people in Filipa Kljajica street. Later, the witness was arrested in Mali Zvornik, Serbia. He complained to the local police as to why he was being arrested in Serbia to be taken to Bosnia. They told him that this could be cleared up later. He was taken to the Alhos factory in Zvornik where Brano Grujic was there, who cursed him, kicked him between his legs. A major who was then one of Arkan's deputies and whom he believes was called by Markovic, entered, punched him in the head, and told him that he would kill him personally. The major seemed to be in charge and shouted at Grujic for allowing people to so easily enter the headquarters. The major told Grujic that this was no way to wage war and that, if this continued, he would take away his 3.800 pieces of artillery. The witness was then taken to the Alhos factory. He was told that he would be -- have to be made an example of and killed. When he was taken into the Alhos factory, he was detained with 20 other Muslim detainees from Zvornik. He waited to be interrogated. Whilst he was waiting, he could hear the screams of the other people from his room who were taken out and also interrogated. When they were returned to the room, they were dumped on the floor, bleeding, unconscious and some of them were dying. He was the last person to be taken for interrogation. He was taken by TO soldiers but the actual interrogation was carried out by Arkan's men. When the witness explained that he was a Serb and that he was only there because he had been too frightened to say when he was stopped, their attitude changed towards him. They then took him out of the room, gave him a sleeping bag, and he was able to lie down with 15 or 20 other of Arkan's men who were lying there fully armed, waiting for morning. In the morning, the witness realised his only chance of escape was when he saw Arkan actually in the Alhos building where the SDS Crisis Staff was staying. He approached Arkan and said that he was a Serb and had been taken there by mistake and he was a driver of a lorry and needed to carry on. Arkan told him to leave, it was okay. When one other driver who was with him asked him what would they do without papers, Arkan simply said, "Tell the people at the barricades that Arkan has let you go." In this way the witness was able to make his escape from Zvornik, made his way to Serbia where he was informed by his family that the local MUP in Serbia had received a fax from Zvornik stating that he'd be arrested and returned to Zvornik. The witness was also told that three Serb military policemen were looking for him. Now, with the permission of the Chamber, I would just like to ask the witness one question orally which I kindly ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: -- the witness to answer, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness 1524, you mention in your statement that you saw men in black uniforms and clothes on the other side of the Drina going into and attacking various apartments. Were you able to recognise from which paramilitary group this -- these people came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524
utterances.text: I am not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question for you. The question is: When you were on the other side of the Drina, you saw men dressed in black paramilitary-type uniforms entering buildings. Were you able to tell from which paramilitary unit these men belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524
utterances.text: Certainly. They belonged to Arkan's units, because the previous day, before the fighting started, I saw them in the region of Karakaj, across the bridge when you enter Bosnia. And later I saw them also when I was arrested. They were wearing those same uniforms as those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were you on the other side of the Drina and how good a view did you have of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524
utterances.text: It could have been about 100 to 150 metres on the outside, and that is quite close enough to see the uniform clearly and the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That would conclude the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to adjourn now. Witness B-1524, I'm sorry we can't finish your evidence. We have to adjourn now. I gather this is not the first time that you've been much inconvenienced in giving evidence. I'm sorry that's so, but we will try and finish on the next occasion, next Tuesday, when you come back. If you would, please, be back at 9.00 then and we will try and finish your evidence. Could you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back then. We will adjourn now until Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of November, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 29071 to 29080.
